bel0: After Lumbar Disc Surgery: Recovery and Exercises | İhsan Eren
bel1: After lumbar disc surgery (microdiscectomy), when can you walk, sit, drive, and go back to work and sport? Warning signs and six exercises for the first weeks.
bel3: Have you had, or are you about to have, surgery for a slipped disc in your lower back (microdiscectomy)? In this operation, the piece of disc pressing on the nerve is removed through a small cut with the help of a microscope. Leg pain often eases straight away, but the back muscles may ache for a while. Staying active and doing the right exercises in the weeks after surgery is the most important part of recovery.

bel11: To get out of bed, first roll onto your side, let your legs drop over the edge of the bed, then push up with your hand and elbow; do not sit straight up.
bel12: When your back hurts, lie down rather than sit: on your front, on your side with a pillow between your knees, or on your back with your knees bent.
bel13: At first, sit on a firm chair for short periods and build up gradually. Do not slouch.
bel14: Avoid sudden twisting and heavy lifting.
bel16: A mild ache after a new activity is acceptable; severe pain is not.
bel17: If you have overdone it and your back is very sore, keep up gentle exercise and walking until the pain settles, then build up again.
bel18: Keep your pain controlled enough to let you move; do not push into pain during exercise.
bel20: Six exercises for the first weeks
bel21: Do the exercises 3–4 times a day. If your surgeon or physiotherapist has given you specific advice, follow that first. If your symptoms get worse, stop the exercise and tell your team.
bel23: Lie on your back with your knees bent. Gently draw in the deep tummy muscles below your belly button and your pelvic floor muscles. Do not hold your breath.
bel24: Hold for 10 seconds if you can, 10 repetitions
bel25: Lie on your back with your knees bent. Gently flatten the hollow of your back towards the bed, then relax.
bel27: Lying on your front and pressing up
bel28: First lie on your front for 3–5 minutes. As it becomes comfortable, come up onto your elbows; later, push up with your arms while your hips stay on the bed. Let your arms do the work, not your back.
bel30: If your pain spread down the back of your leg before surgery, you can start this from day 2–3. Sit upright and slowly straighten your knee until you feel a gentle pull at the back of your leg, hold briefly, then bend it.
bel32: If your surgeon agrees, you can start walking on the day of surgery. Take short, frequent walks rather than a few long ones; stand tall and build up the time gradually.
bel34: While lying or sitting, pull your toes up towards you, then point them down. This helps the circulation in your legs.
bel36: When you can make an emergency stop and sit comfortably for the whole journey; this usually takes at least 4–6 weeks. Make sure your pain is well controlled and ask your surgeon about the exact timing.
bel37: When can I go back to work?
bel38: It depends on your job. The NHS says usually 4–6 weeks; according to one NHS leaflet, you may return to desk work after 6–8 weeks and to heavy manual work after at least 3 months, sometimes 6. Decide with your surgeon.
bel40: According to one NHS leaflet, once the wound has healed you can swim freestyle or backstroke from week 4, cycle and walk briskly from 4–6 weeks, and play golf and gentle tennis from 3 months. Avoid running and heavy lifting for the first 6 months.
bel41: Does an exercise programme after surgery help?
bel42: According to a Cochrane review of 22 randomised trials and 2,503 people, exercise programmes starting 4–6 weeks after surgery improved pain and daily function in the short term more than no treatment. Intensive programmes were slightly more effective than mild ones; there was no difference between supervised and home programmes. In no study did exercise increase the rate of re-operation. The quality of the evidence ranged from low to very low.
bel44: Serious complications are rare. They include leakage of spinal fluid, nerve damage, back pain that does not go away and slipping of the vertebrae; some may need further surgery. Leg pain often eases straight away, but the back muscles may ache for a while.

bel47: If you have difficulty passing urine, or have lost control of your bladder or bowels
bel48: If you have new numbness, weakness or pain in your legs or both feet that is different from before surgery

bel50: If there is warmth, itching, redness or discharge around the wound
bel51: In the first three situations, go to A&E without delay. In the others, contact your surgical team.
